Analysis by Richard Cowan

Last November, the NORML Weekly News featured a story about a federal report predicting that marijuana prices were going to fall. 

See 

Annotated NORML Weekly News – November 15, 2007. Sativex Relieves Pain for Patients; Will It Cause Pain for Prohibitionists? Bear Market for Cannabis? Calling All Lawyers to Key West. 

and 

Where Have All the BC Buds Gone? Tighter Borders and Falling Greenback Reveal Illusion of Prohibition Fostered by Both Sides. BS After All? 

I am going to be doing a survey of my friends who are in a position to know, and I would like to hear from readers about any change in prices that they have observed.

However, today I would like to explore the implications of the weak global economy’s impact on the whole of cannabis prohibition, not just prices. 

For example, it is generally agreed that the Great Depression played a significant role in hastening the end of alcohol prohibition. I doubt that the current downturn is likely to be as severe as the early 1930s, but alcohol prohibition was not as expensive as the Drug War is today. 

Unlike the federal government, the states have to balance their operating budgets and they are especially vulnerable to drops in property and sales tax revenues. 

Consider the situation in two very different states. California is facing a $16 billion budget deficit and Kentucky is looking at a $1.3 billion shortfall. Consequently, California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger proposed saving $400 million by releasing more than 22,000 inmates who had less than 20 months remaining on their sentences. Kentucky legislators have approved the early release of perhaps 2,000 prisoners to save nearly $50 million. 

In case you are wondering about the math, Kentucky spends more than $18,600 per inmate per year, but California spends an average of $46,104 per prisoner. One of those numbers is scandalous, and perhaps both are. 

See 

The Drug Testing and Rehab Rackets Keep Prisons Full. From California to the UK The Results Are Tragic – And Expensive. Did Michael Vick Find A Loophole? 

Generally speaking, crime goes up with the unemployment rate, which is already very high in the inner cities. This means that the police and courts are going to be facing increasing work loads just as local budgets begin to tighten. Jails are a part of the city and county budgets, and they often have to absorb the overflow from the state prisons. This problem pushes the costs down ever closer to the taxpayers. 

The problem is hardly confined to the US. Last month, The London Telegraph reported that two terrorists were released early because of overcrowding in prohibitionist Britain’s prisons. 

According to the Telegraph, the early release program “was brought in as an emergency measure to ease pressures on the system caused by a record rise in the number of prisoners to more than 80,000… More than 20,000 offenders have been released early since the scheme came into effect last summer.” 

Of course, these problems did not keep the Tories from squealing about a decline in the number of cannabis dealers sent to prison, but it is clear that the British courts are sensitive to the problems in the system, even if the politicians are not. 

By contrast, figures from Statistics Netherlands show that at the end of last year 14,450 people were being held in Dutch prisons, down more than 10 percent since 2006. For the second consecutive year there has been a drop in the number of prisoners. Criminologists attribute this drop to a strong decline in the number of 'petty' crimes, such as burglary and theft. Fifty-five percent of all inmates are of foreign descent, a percentage that has remained stable for several years. Of course, we should remember that – with the exception of cannabis possession and retail sales – The Netherlands practices its own form of prohibition. 

See 

International “Prohibition Situation Report” – DEAland Media Ignore News Showing Cannabis Prohibition Is Counterproductive. Coffee Shop System Survives. and 

Dutch Lessons: Tolerance Works. Prohibition Is Counterproductive. Who Is The Real Threat To Our Freedom and Security? 

It is clear that the Drug War is creating the same problems around the world, and at some point, we will have to start counting its cost, and especially the cost of the increasingly unpopular war on cannabis users. 

In the meantime, consider the impact of different trends on cannabis prices. 

1. For non-medical users, cannabis is a “luxury” item which smokers might forgo, which would put downward pressure on prices, and/or increase the relative demand for Mexican commercial over higher quality domestic production. 

2. Increased enforcement of immigration laws will put more pressure on poor Mexicans, whose job prospects in the US are worsening. This will tend to encourage smuggling contraband as opposed to smuggling people, thereby increasing the supply of Mexican commercial. 

3. On the other hand, the escalation of the Drug War in Mexico will increase risk premiums on marijuana, and increase costs on both sides of the border.

4. Increased unemployment may encourage more people to try to grow their own as away of keeping their homes. Also, the huge number of homes being sold in foreclosure creates more opportunities for indoor growing. 

5. The increased recognition of the medical value of cannabis will increase demand, especially among the rapidly growing cohort of aging baby-boomers. 

6. Increased enforcement against domestic growers in Florida and elsewhere will reduce supply and increase prices, because the prohibitionist police state will not stop until it is forced to. 

The point is that there are strongly conflicting forces at work in the cannabis market. How will they balance out? Supply and demand are fundamental to all markets, but in inefficient contraband markets they are much more difficult to measure. 

Again, please email me your own thoughts and experiences with current market trends. Cowan@MarijuanaNews.com
